title: Noor and the Hymn
premise: Ines Vasquez hosts a graveyard-shift call-in show whose listeners all died the week before, and he keeps broadcasting because the dead still need someone to count their doors and keep their lights on. When an excavation crew unearths a door sealed from the inside beneath the old hymn hall, Ines is pulled into the building's memory, where the last living resident, Miss Odile, is preparing to sign papers that will sell the hall — and its song — to men who want the final verse for themselves. The verse is a hymn that grants power over whoever hears it sung whole; Ines must learn it without ever singing along, while deciding whether loyalty to his ghostly callers matters more than the truth of what they did to earn their deaths. In the end, Ines refuses to sign in Odile's place, teaches the verse only to the dead so they can finally finish singing it themselves, and walks out as the hall collapses into silence — alive, alone, and no longer needed.
about_author: Mara Crane is the pen name of a former late-night radio producer who spent six years answering calls from strangers who couldn't sleep. She writes horror about buildings that remember and people who stay too long.

chapters.title: Dead Air, Live Callers
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. We meet the 3 a.m. show: Ines takes calls from listeners he knows died last week, calmly logging each one, keeping studio lights on and counting doors per an old station superstition. The emotional beat is eerie tenderness — he grieves them by doing his job perfectly.

chapters.title: The Excavation
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. A crew digging beside the derelict Hymn Hall unearths a door sealed from the inside, scratched with tally marks. That night every caller goes silent mid-sentence at once. Beat: dread arrives on schedule, and Ines realizes the dead are afraid.

chapters.title: Miss Odile Signs Nothing Yet
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. The hall's last resident, ninety-one and lucid, receives the developers' papers and refuses, humming a fragment of the hymn. She recognizes Ines's voice from the radio. Beat: stubborn dignity masking terror of what finishing the song would do.

chapters.title: Pulled Through
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Investigating the door, Ines touches the tally marks and is drawn inside the hall's memory — a version of the building where his dead callers now live as residents. Beat: disorientation curdling into belonging; found family offered too easily.

chapters.title: The Verse They Kept
chapters.summary: Odile's POV, interwoven with Ines's. Flashback reveals the choir deliberately never sang the final verse aloud; those who heard it whole became obedient, then hollow. The excavation crew's foreman already hums it under his breath. Beat: power revealed as infection.

chapters.title: Doors, Counted
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. Inside the memory-hall, Ines resumes his ritual — lights, door counts — and the residents begin to trust him. But he notices new doors appearing, one per caller, each locked from the resident's side. Beat: warmth shadowed by the cost of staying.

chapters.title: Loyalty's Invoice
chapters.summary: Odile's POV. The foreman offers Odile freedom from the hall if she signs and gives up the verse; she nearly does, until she hears him sing two lines to a worker who stops blinking. Beat: loyalty vs. truth — her silence protected people, but silence is running out.

chapters.title: The Last Resident
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. The residents reveal the truth: they weren't victims; they sang the verse once, willingly, to keep the hall's power contained, and died holding it. They ask Ines to take Odile's place as keeper. Beat: betrayal reframed as sacrifice; temptation peaks.

chapters.title: Without Singing Along
chapters.summary: Climax, alternating POV. The foreman forces the door open with a partial choir; Odile begins signing the papers as the hymn swells toward completion. Ines learns the final verse — mouthing it, never voicing it — and teaches it wordlessly to the dead, who rise and sing it themselves, unmaking the foreman's borrowed power. Beat: sacrifice without surrender.

chapters.title: Sign-Off
chapters.summary: Ines's POV. The unsigned papers burn; Odile dies peacefully as the hall finishes its song and folds shut behind its own door. Ines broadcasts one last show to static, thanks his listeners, and signs off at dawn. Beat: grief resolved into release — he was family, not keeper, and the family let him go.
